messages.content:
Rate the following clinical vignette:

Here is a clinical vignette written from the perspective of a treating psychologist.

Patient: Kofi, 19-year-old male
Occupation: Detective

Kofi is a thoughtful young man who presents with a still, watchful quality that feels older than his nineteen years. He speaks in a low, measured tone, often pausing to scan the room before he continues, as if verifying the safety of the space. He is a detective for a major metropolitan police force, a position he earned through an accelerated cadet program for exceptional candidates. He has been with the department for just over a year.

His story begins six months ago, during a plainclothes operation that went catastrophically wrong. Kofi was working a sting on a human trafficking network. The plan was to pose as a potential buyer. The plan was sound. But the network had an informant inside the department. Kofi was taken.

He remembers the van. The smell of diesel and stale sweat. The hood over his head. He was held for eleven days in a basement. The details of what happened there are still fragmented, surfacing in his mind like wreckage after a flood. He speaks of the concrete floor, the single lightbulb, the constant sound of water dripping. He speaks of the men who guarded him, their faces always in shadow, their voices flat and without emotion. He was kept in a small cage, barely tall enough to stand. He was fed once a day, a bowl of cold rice. He was interrogated for information he did not have. He was beaten when they did not believe him.

He was rescued in a raid, found curled in the corner of his cage. He remembers the flash of the breaching charge, the shouting, the feeling of a large hand-a colleague's hand-on his shoulder, pulling him out. He remembers the blinding light of the sun.

Now, Kofi is back at work, but he is not the same detective. The sharp, intuitive edge that made him a prodigy is gone, replaced by a hyper-vigilant, exhausting caution. He cannot walk into an interrogation room without his heart hammering against his ribs. The smell of stale coffee in the precinct's break room-a smell he once loved-now makes his stomach clench, transporting him back to the basement. He has started to flinch at sudden movements from his colleagues. Last week, when his partner playfully clapped him on the back, Kofi spun around with his hand on his service weapon. The look of shock on his partner's face haunts him.

He has trouble sleeping. When he does, he dreams of the dripping water, the cage. He wakes up in a cold sweat, his girlfriend, Maya, trying to soothe him. She is patient, he says, but he can see the worry in her eyes. He has pulled away from her. He feels like a contaminated thing, unworthy of her touch. Their intimacy has evaporated. He cannot bear to be held, because being held feels like being trapped.

At work, he has started to avoid the basement evidence lockers. He makes excuses. He takes the stairs instead of the elevator, needing to feel the exertion of his own legs. He carries a small, sharpened pencil in his pocket at all times-a secret talisman, a tiny weapon.

He scored a 63 on the PCL-5, which reflects the severe, pervasive nature of his symptoms. But to Kofi, those numbers are just numbers. What is real is the way he cannot sit with his back to a door. What is real is the way he has stopped laughing. What is real is the feeling that the cage is still there, invisible but absolute, and he is still inside it, even when he is standing in the middle of a busy street. He is a detective who can no longer trust the world to be what it seems.

The smell of stale coffee in the precinct's break room—a smell he once loved—now makes his stomach clench, transporting him back to the basement' is highly specific, linking a clear behavioral avoidance and a sensory trigger to a vivid emotional and physiological response. This level of precision demonstrates why the vignette is extremely clear.
